speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: I don't use the word hero lightly. Congressman John Robert Lewis is a hero. In the turbulent 1960s, young John Lewis stood side by side with Martin Luther King, Jr., and other civil rights crusaders, displaying unwavering courage. Through years of continual nonviolent protests, John Lewis battled segregation. head on and shine a spotlight on the cruelty of racism in America. Whether he was participating in sit-ins and Nashville, marching for equality in Washington, D.C., taking a stand on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, or proudly serving his district in Atlanta, John Lewis has always embodied persistence, fearlessness, and hope. The son of Alabama sharecroppers, John Lewis, grew up witnessing the injustices of the Jim Crow South. It was here that he began his life's work to fight for equality and justice for everybody. Everybody has a story and there is something to be learned from every experience. Use your life as a class This is Masterclass with Congressman John Lewis.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: I grew up in rural Alabama about 10 miles from a little town called Troy. In 1944, when I was four years old, and I do remember when I was four, my father had saved $300. And with the $300, a man sold him 110 acres of land. On the form, I fell in love with raising chickens, putting my mother, a father wanted to have a chicken for lunch, for dinner, I didn't like it, and I would boycott the meal. But the chickens became my friends. And as a little boy, I wanted to be a minister. So, with the help of my brothers and sisters and cousins, we got all of our chickens together in the chicken yard. They would help make up the audience, the congregation. And I would start preaching to these chickens. I wanted to stay the souls of some of these chickens. And I would tell them, I said, be good. Be kind. Not to fight. And some of these chickens were about their heads. Some of the chickens shaped their heads. They never quite said, amen. But they tended to listen to me much better than some of my colleagues listened to me today in the Congress. I grew up with, I guess, a restless spirit. When we would go off to school, we had the broken down school buses. And all of the little black children had to go down and attend the police staff schools. And all of the little white children went to another school. I saw the signs that said white men, colored men, white women, colored women. I didn't like what I saw. And I thought things would be better. And when I was 15 years old, I heard Martin Luther King Jr. on radio. Listen to Dr. King inspired me. He gave me hope. And I kept up with the drama that was taking place around the country. What was happening in Montgomery and about the Supreme Court decision in 1954. And I dream of going to a better school, riding a better bus. I didn't like the fact that my father and my grandparents, my uncles and aunts, didn't have any rights. My mother was serving over again. Boy, that's the way it is. She was saying, you know, cool it. Be quiet. Don't get in trouble. Well, I was inspired to get in trouble, to get in good trouble. Good trouble is simple. When you see something that is not right, not fair, not just, you have a moral obligation, you have a mission, you have a mandate to speak up, to speak out. You may get arrested. and taken to jail, you may be beaten and left bloody. And you could be murdered. You could die. But it's part of the price that you have to pay, not just to liberate yourself, but have free and liberate others. I have been a scepter at college in Nashville, Tennessee. By this time, I'm 18 years old, an uncle of mine gave me $100 bill, more money than I ever had. gave me a footlocker. I put everything that I own, accepted those chickens in that footlocker and took a Greyhound bus to Nashville, Tennessee. I remember so well meeting Jim Lawson, young Methodist minister. He represented an organization called a Fellowship of Reconciliation. He had studied the philosophy and the discipline of nonviolence. In the fall of 1959, he saw conducting these unbelievable training sessions. A small group of students would come, listen to him, go through role play, and we would help what we call social drama. Because black people and white people couldn't be seated together in a theater. Black people had to go upstairs. White people went downstairs. You couldn't be seated together in a restaurant at a lunch counter. We wanted to change that. We started sitting here on a regular basis. You'd be sitting there in an orderly, peaceful, non-violent fashion. Someone would come up and spit on us, or put a lighting cigarette out in our hair, pull hot water, hot coffee, and pull us off the stools. We have what we call the do's and don'ts of the city movement. If someone pushed you, don't push back. If someone cursed you, do not curse. You wanted to project that it was something that the community could rally around and support. White people cursing, making a lot of noise. These young men and women. or just sitting there in an orderly, peaceful fashion. Non-violence is not the absence of violence. It is the presence of justice. It is the presence of bringing the dirt and the filth from under the rug, out of the corners, into the open light so we can deal with it. To help convince people who may be standing on their sidelines or who may be watching, that this is the right thing to do. And the sit-in spread around the South like wildfire. And we were told over and over again, if we continued to sit in, we would be arrested. And I wanted to be prepared if I were going to get arrested and go to jail. I wanted to look what some young people would call a sharp. a fresh, a clean. I wanted a new suit to wear to jail. I had very little money, so I went downtown and asked for it to use men's store and bought a suit. I paid $5 for that suit. On that day, 89 students were arrested. Became the first mass arrest in the city movement. We feel the city jail. And we conducted nonviolent workshops while we were in jail. We sang songs. It created a sense of solidarity that we became one big family. Jim Lawson taught us the whole concept of the beloved community. That this idea that in the bosom of every human being, there is this spark of divinity. that is this spark or something that is sacred and holy and special and that we don't have a right to destroy it. You know, no one want to go to jail. No one want to be beaten. No one want to feel pain. But you come to that point, you have what I call an executive session with yourself. Say, if just the price, you must pay. for people to be free, to be liberated, to be whole, then we must be prepared to pay that price. When I was arrested, I felt liberated. I felt free. I felt like I had crossed over. And I did look clean. I did look sharp. I did look fresh. And I have not looked back since.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: One of John Lewis' boldest decisions was to become one of the original 13 Freedom Riders. The U.S. Supreme Court had already ruled that segregation and interstate travel was unconstitutional. But in many places, those laws simply weren't being enforced. And so in 1961, John Lewis and other civil rights activists decided to get on a bus to challenge segregation in the racially divided South. They nearly got themselves killed in the process. John Lewis knew full well the danger and the difficulty of what he was getting into. But to hear him tell it, the freedom rides were something that simply had to be done. He was 21 years old.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: The Freedom Ride came into being on the part of an organization called Core, the Congress of Racial Equality. It was to test a decision of the United States Supreme Court, then in racial discrimination during interstate travel, because like people and white people couldn't be seated together. to travel through Virginia, through North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, to New Orleans. We made the decision with coal and other groups that we will organize the Freedom Rides, stored in May of 1961. I was 21 years old, came to Washington. A group of us went to a little Chinese restaurant in Washington, D.C. Now growing up in rural Alabama, going to school in Nashville, Tennessee, I never had Chinese food before. We had this wonderful, unbelievable meal. But someone said that evening, you should eat well because this may be like the last supper. On May 4th, we left that morning on the Greyhound bus to go from Washington, D.C. all the way to New Orleans. When we arrived in a little town called Rock Hill, South Carolina, we got off the bus, went into this waiting room walk, white waiting. A group of young men, members of the Klan attacked us, beat us, and left us lying in a pool of blood. The bus was burned in Aniston, Alabama. Another bus was burned and people were beaten in Birmingham. And then Montgomery, Alabama, and Engamaw, I met at the Greyhound bus station. They first jumped on members of the press. So if you had a camera, a pad, you would first want to be attacked. And then they turned on us. My seepmate on that deck of the ride was a young white student. We both were beaten in left line in the street, bloody. I had to get a patch of my head. My seatmate was in the hospital. Eventually, Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Reverend Rath Abernathy came to Montgomery, they heard about the Freedom Rides, they heard what had happened. We had a meeting with him, said we're going to have a mass meeting, and supported the Freedom Rides. At the Fresh Baptist Church in downtown Montgomery, there was an attempt to burn the church. the more than 1,500 people in the church. The city of Montgomery was put on the martial law, and then we made a decision to leave Montgomery and travel to Mississippi. And going to Mississippi, I had never been there before, but I grew up here in Mississippi, was worse than the state of Alabama. This is the state where Emmett Till was lynched. This is the state where people came up missing. So the National Guard took us to the Mississippi State Line, and you get to Mississippi, the Mississippi State Troopers put us in jail, black and white freedom riders. Then they made a decision to take us all to parchment state penitentiary. A guy is standing there with his rifle, and he said, we have niggas here. They would eat you. They would beat you. Just saying your damn freedom songs now, they said to each one of us, take all of your clothing. It was an attempt to dehumanize us. They segregated us, put all of the white men in one cell block, all of the black men in another. They did the same thing for the white and black women. And most of us stayed in jail there for 44 days. But the Freedom Ride led to the segregation of public transportation all across the South. President Kennedy, the Attorney General of Robert Kennedy was able to get the Interstate Commerce Commission to issue an order, taking nine old signs that said white weighting, colored weighting in the deep South. More than any lesson left learned, you have to be consistent. You have to learn to be not just persistent, but also insistent. And if you see something that need to be done, do it. It may be hard, it may be difficult, but keep the faith. Hang in there. The march on Washington was the idea of a Philip Randolph, this dean of black leadership, a man who had been wanting to see a march on Washington since the days of Roosevelt. President Kennedy was to the White House to meet with him. Kennedy. They liked the idea. He said, if you bring all these people to Washington, won't there be violence and chaos and disorder? Mr. Randolph responded to his baritone voice and said, Mr. President, orderly, peaceful, non-violent protests. And we stood organizing. We were able to bring more than 250,000 people to Washington. And we all had to prepare a speech. I was very young, 23 years old, hit all of my hair and a few pounds lighter. When A. Philarendoff said and I present to you young John Lewis, the National Chairman of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, I looked to my right. I saw hundreds and hundreds of young people who had been involved during the early days looked straight ahead, I saw this sea of humanity. Then I looked to the left. I saw young, black men and young, white men up in the trees trying to get a better view. And then I said to myself, well, this is it. And I looked straight ahead again, and something said to me, go for it. And I opened my mouth, and I started speaking. And some people thought that my speech was a little strong. That was too radical. But I thought it was rather a good statement. And then, Martin Luther King Jr. came up as the tenth speaker. I've heard Dr. King speak and preach so many times. But on that day, he was on fire. He spoke out of the depth of his soul. He preached a sermon. He turned the steps of the Lincoln Memorial into a modern-day pool of pit, and he knew he was doing it. We all lifted up. When the march was all over, President Kennedy invited us down to the White House. He was beaming like a private father, and he kept saying to each one of us, you did a good job, you did a good job. And when he got to Dr. King, he said, you did a good job, and you had a dream. That was my last time seeing President Kennedy. Dr. King used to say that a time is always right to protest of what is right. He also said that's not anything more powerful than the margin of a determined people. I felt the end, and I feel today that the vote is precious. is almost sacred. It is the most powerful, nonviolent instrument or tool that we have in a democratic society. But for many years, people of color could not register to vote, especially in the 11 states that all confederacy. People stood in unmovable lines. People were beaten. People were murdered for attempting to register or to encourage others to register. In one little county called Lowndes County, the county was more than 80% African-American, just outside of Montgomery, Alabama. There was not a single registered African-American voter in the county. As the President Johnson signed this civil rights act in July 1964, we said to him in effect, Mr. President, we need a voting rights act. He said, I just signed this to the right side. We don't have the votes in the Congress to get a voting right side. If you want it, make me do it. That was a protest in Perry County, Alabama. A young man was shot and murdered because of what happened to him. We made a decision to attempt to march from Selma to Montgomery. And someone from Dr. King's organization said, John, we want you to march with us. We want you to lead this march with Jose Williams from Dr. King's organization. We left church, we conducted a nonviolent workshop in a courtyard, and then we lined up in twos to walk from Selma to Montgomery. I was wearing a backpack before it became fashionable to wear backpacks. I thought I was going to get arrested and go to jail, so in this backpack, I wanted to have something to eat. I had one apple and one orange. I had two books. at toothpaste and a toothbrush. But we understood why we were walking through the streets of Selma, that the sheriff of Selma and Dallas County had requested that all white men over the age of 21 to come down to the courthouse at Saturday night to be depetized to become part of his posse. We just kept walking. We come to the highest point on the Edmonton Bridge Down below, we see a sea of blue Alabama State Troopers. We saw all of this water down below in Alabama River. Jose Williams said to me, John, can you swim? I said, no, Jose. What about you? He said a little. I said, well, that's too much water in this river for us to jump. We must go straight ahead. A man by the name of John Cloud identified himself and said, I'm Major John Cloud of the Alabama State Troopers. This was an unlawful march, would not be allowed to continue. Just first, return to your homes or to your church. As a Major, may I have a word? There will be no word. You saw these men putting on their gas masks. He said, Troopers advance. They came toward us, beating us with night sticks. Tramping us with horses. releasing tear gas. I was the first person to be hit. I was hitting a hit by a state trooper with a night stick. I thought I saw death. I thought I was going to down that bridge. I thought it was my last nonviolent protest. And all these many years later, I don't recall I made it back across that bridge to the church. I do recall being in the church They asked me to say something to the audience, and I stood up and said something like, I don't understand it. Our President Johnson can send troops to Vietnam and can not send troops to Selma, Alabama to protect people who only desire to register to vote. And the next thing I knew had been taken to the Good Samaritan Hospital in Selma, where 17 of us have been hospitalized. And early, The next day, that Monday morning, morning to the cane junior, came by to see me. And Dr. King said, don't worry, John. We will make it from Selma to Montgomery. I was hopeful. I was optimistic. I never lost a sense of hope. Even being in pain or being in jail, you have to have hope. When you lose that sense of hope, that sense of optimism, it's like giving up. President Johnson spoke to a joint session of the Congress, spoke to the nation. And made one of the most meaningful speeches, any American president that made him more than time. I was sitting in the room with Martin Luther King Jr. and others. And I looked at him. Tears came by his face. And I think we all cried a little. Because we knew it was just a matter of time. The Congress would pass a voting rightsite. and President Johnson was signed at Interlo. So I was there on August 6, 1965. When you signed it, I gave me one of the pins to the youth to sign it. My mother and my father were able to register and vote for the first time. My father in particular, when he became very, very proud And I think in places, it was dangerous for him to sit, to hold me. But he said it. He was, yes, that's my boy. For me, Dr. King was my hero. Also, he was my friend. He was like a big brother. You know, he gave me a way out. Maybe a way in. But he made life better. He was just a warmest, nicest guy you ever wanted to meet. He would tease me from time to time. He would say things like, John, do you stay a preach? And I said, Dr. King, when I'm taking a shower, and he thought it was so funny, he would just laugh. And on occasion, when we would be traveling in Alabama or someplace in Mississippi, you see a little hole in the wall, cafe, a restaurant. He would say things like, we should stop and get something to eat. We get arrested and go to jail, we go on the full stomach. And he thought it was so funny, but I didn't think it was so funny. He had a heart of gold. The day that Dr. King was assassinated, April 4, 1960, It was working at Robert Kennedy Campaign for the Democratic nomination for president. And when Robert Kennedy got up to speak, you said he had some sad news. Like many, many people waiting to hear Robert Kennedy, we all cried. It was a sad and dark hour. I didn't know what was happening to this country, really. I felt like something had died in America. And I think something died in all of us. One of the reasons for getting involved in American politics to run for office, I felt maybe just maybe that I could help continue the efforts of Dr. King. As we said in the movement, you must continue to pick him up and put him down. believe that somehow and some way we're going to overcome, we're going to survive. It may get knocked down, but you got to get up. You dry your tears and keep moving. During the freedom rides or during the sit-ins, during my efforts in Mississippi, around the vote, working in Selma, I never, ever thought about giving up. and saying it's too much. I never thought about dropping out. You come to that point where you say, I got to go on and see what they ain't going to be. You have to. You have to get out there and push and pull to try to make things better for generations yet unborn. Each one of us has the ability to resist. Not to be quiet. We have to be brave. We have to be bold. We have to use our constitutional rights. If it means a march, a silent walk, a sit-in, a sit-down, a maybe signing a petition right in the letter of voting, we have to be engaged, all of us, as members of the human family, as citizens of this country. There are forces that want to take us back to another place, and we're saying we're not going back. But come too far, we made too much progress to stop not or to turn around. That's why I feel it is part of my obligation, my mission, or mandate to reach as many young people as possible. The fight is not over. We have to continue to fight. And sometimes you have to fight some of the old battles over and over again for the next generation, for generation yet unborn. You too can make a contribution and you must.

explicit_propositions.text: The Freedom Ride was organized by CORE, the Congress of Racial Equality, in May 1961.
The Freedom Ride aimed to test the U.S. Supreme Court’s ruling against racial segregation in interstate travel.
The Freedom Riders traveled from Washington, D.C., through several Southern states including Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Alabama, and Mississippi, ending in New Orleans.
In Rock Hill, South Carolina, the Freedom Riders were attacked by Klansmen upon exiting a bus terminal.
A bus was burned in Anniston, Alabama, and another in Birmingham, Alabama, during the Freedom Ride.
In Montgomery, Alabama, the Freedom Riders faced violent attacks, and attempts were made to burn the church where they gathered.
The National Guard escorted the Freedom Riders to the Mississippi border, where they were arrested by Mississippi State Troopers.
Freedom Riders were imprisoned at Parchman State Penitentiary, subjected to dehumanizing treatment and segregation by race and gender.
The Freedom Ride ultimately led to the desegregation of public transportation across the South via an Interstate Commerce Commission order.
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and Rev. Ralph Abernathy supported the Freedom Riders after learning of the violence they endured.

assumptions.text: Nonviolent resistance is morally justified and effective even under extreme physical danger.

The legitimacy of democracy depends on universal access to the ballot and protection of voting rights.
Violence against activists, while tragic, does not invalidate the righteousness of their cause.
Hope and persistence are necessary psychological foundations for sustained activism.
Continuity between past struggles and future actions is vital; movements must be passed forward across generations.
